reason: The text explicitly emphasizes hierarchical relationships through multiple structural elements: (1) the master-servant relationship, with Abraham's servant explicitly described as 'master of his house' (מֹשֵׁל בְּכָל־ אֲשֶׁר־ לוֹ) yet fully subordinate to Abraham; (2) the paternal authority of Abraham, who commands his servant and controls the arrangement of his son's marriage; (3) the formal gesture of submission when the servant swears an oath by placing his hand under Abraham's thigh (יָדְךָ תַּחַת יְרֵכִֽי), a ritual expression of deference; (4) Isaac's relationship as the rightful heir in the family structure; and (5) the authority of Rebekah's father and brother to release her to marriage. Throughout the narrative, the hierarchy is reinforced through acts of obedience, deference, and the consistent use of titles like 'master' (אֲדֹנִי) and decision-making authority flowing downward through familial and social ranks.
